inline.s: The Sutra of Immeasurable Pure and Equal Enlightenment Spoken by the Buddha (Han translation) says:

“Once one opens through and attains clear comprehension, within the natural there is the mark of the natural, and the natural has its root and foundation. Naturally there come to be five lights up to nine colors; the five lights up to nine colors intermingle and revolve, changing through hundreds and thousands of transformations — the most surpassing naturalness. Naturally the seven treasures are formed, gathered and clasped into all things; the lights and essences intermingle in brightness, all bringing forth excellence, of a beauty beyond all measure.”
The Sutra of Amitābha, the Perfectly Awakened Buddha of the Sala Grove, Who Delivers Beings on the Human Path (Wu translation) says:
“In the naturalness of Uttarakuru, the seven treasures are naturally formed, gathered and clasped into all things.”
“Uttarakuru”:

Uttarakuru, also written Auttarakuru, is the northern continent of Uttarakuru. “The northern continent of Uttarakuru”: it is one of the four great continents of the Sahā world (Pūrvavideha in the east, Jambudvīpa in the south, Aparagodānīya in the west, and Uttarakuru in the north), lying to the north of Mount Sumeru, where the people are peaceful and happy and live a thousand years. “Uttarakuru becomes the seven treasures, gathered and clasped into all things”: the prelude to seeing one’s nature clearly (to penetratingly beholding the intrinsic nature) is the non-arising of a single thought (what the text above calls “truly pure and undefiled”); the state at that time is peaceful and happy (what the text above calls “calm samādhi and peace”), and so Uttarakuru, the northern continent whose people are peaceful and happy, is used as a simile. Once one sees one’s nature clearly (“once one opens through and attains clear comprehension”) and enters the realm of a new heaven and a new earth, this is a leap in kind; hence the transformation “Uttarakuru becomes the seven treasures” is used as a simile. “Gathered and clasped into all things” describes how at that time all things flow forth naturally from the one great treasury of radiance.
The passage below once again urges and exhorts us toward rebirth. This is the World-Honored One’s repeated admonition, his compassion without end.

“Each should strive with diligence, and seek the Way by his own effort. You shall surely transcend and pass beyond, reborn in the land of Amitābha, immeasurable and pure. Cutting across the five destinies, the evil paths close of themselves. The unsurpassed and wondrous Way is easy to go, yet none go there; that land turns no one away — it is the natural pull that draws them on. Let go your aims as though they were empty space, and diligently walk the Way, seeking its virtue. You may gain life beyond measure, with bliss and years that have no end. Why cling to the affairs of the world, why such
náo
clamor — the worry over impermanence?”

The Land of Ultimate Bliss is so surpassing that each of you should strive with diligence, and seek rebirth there by his own effort. You shall surely transcend the three realms and be reborn in the land of Amitābha, immeasurable and pure — the Land of Ultimate Bliss — and so escape the six paths of rebirth. This incomparable golden road, rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, is easy to go yet none go there: the Land of Ultimate Bliss refuses no one who would be reborn there; those beings who are not reborn there are simply drawn along by their own deluded thoughts at the moment of death, and so naturally fall into the six paths and take birth again. Therefore you must surely let go of all conditions, your mind like empty space (let go your aims as though they were empty space), and diligently practice the Pure Land Dharma-gate. Once reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, you gain life eternal, with long life and bliss without limit. Why then be greedy and attached to the affairs of the world, and live in fear and trembling over the coming of death (impermanence)?
“The evil paths close of themselves”: here the evil paths are
those “five evil paths” spoken of in the Sutra of Immeasurable Life (Wei translation): hells, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, and gods. The Sutra of Immeasurable Life (Wei translation) says:

“Each should strive with diligence, and seek it by his own effort. You shall surely transcend and pass beyond, reborn in the Land of Peace and Bliss. Cutting across the five evil paths, the roads of destiny close of themselves. Rising on the Way without end or limit, easy to go yet none go there; that land turns no one away — it is the natural pull that draws them on. Why not cast off worldly affairs, and diligently walk the Way, seeking its virtue? You may gain life beyond measure, with bliss and years that have no end.”

“Five evil paths” are: hells, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, and gods. Because these five paths are the road of birth-and-death and rebirth, for a cultivator who would end birth-and-death and escape the three realms, all of them are evil paths.

“Easy to go yet none go there”: the “easy to go” here is spoken in contrast to other Dharma-gates. In the Chan school, for example, one must pass through the ten thousand thoughts returning to one (which corresponds to the single-mindedness of the Pure Land school), then the one returning to nothing, then seeing one’s nature clearly, and afterward undertake the work of safeguarding and sustaining it, cutting off all affliction utterly — only then can one end birth-and-death and escape rebirth. The Pure Land Dharma-gate, by contrast, requires only ten continuous thoughts at the moment of death, and one can be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss and end birth-and-death and escape rebirth; therefore it is called “easy to go.”
The Jiāxiáng Commentary says:
“By cultivating only the accomplishment of ten thoughts
(the accomplishment of ten continuous thoughts at the moment of death)
one attains rebirth — yet those who practice it are rare
(yet those who earnestly put it into practice are very few).
Hence it is said, ‘easy to go yet none go there.’”
“That land turns no one away; it is the natural pull that draws them on”: the Sutra of Immeasurable Life (Wei translation) says:
“That land turns no one away
(the Land of Ultimate Bliss refuses no sentient being who would be reborn there)
, and it is the natural pull that draws them on
(those sentient beings who are not reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss follow their own deluded thoughts at the moment of death and are drawn naturally to take birth in the six paths)
“Six paths”: hells, hungry ghosts, animals, asuras, humans, and gods. “Virtue”: the true Dharma is called the Way; to gain the Way and not lose it is called virtue. “Clamor (
náo
) clamor”: the appearance of a heart full of restless fear.

“Those sentient beings who are not reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss follow their own deluded thoughts at the moment of death and are drawn naturally to take birth in the six paths”: on this point, Master Lianchi teaches in his Commentary and Notes on the Amitābha Sutra:
Those who are confused at the end of life
, because in ordinary times they follow delusive thoughts, do not cultivate right mindfulness, and their minds are much distracted. At the moment when warmth is about to leave the body
(when the four elements are dissolving)

, everything done in a lifetime appears before them; their mind and spirit are terrified, and their movements and bearing are wild. One who is to enter the hells sees the mountain of knives and the forest of swords as a lovely garden. One who is to fall among animals takes the mare’s womb and the donkey’s foetus for a splendid hall. Even one who has done good and is to be reborn as a human or a god cannot escape loving or hating his parents. Even a lesser sage at the stage of initial resolve cannot yet know his entering and departing with right knowledge. All of this is what is called confusion. Riding on this confusion, they receive rebirth in the seven destinies of the three realms according to their karma.

As the Buddha said: ‘When the mind is pure, the Buddha-land is pure.’ He also said: ‘All lands are upheld by thought alone.’ When the pure thought is accomplished, one will certainly be reborn — of this there is no doubt.”
(For further teachings, see
Right Mindfulness at the Time of Death

Translation: Those who are confused at the end of life are so because in ordinary times they follow delusive thoughts, do not cultivate right mindfulness, and their minds are much distracted. When the four elements dissolve, everything done in a lifetime appears before them; their mind and spirit are terrified and their bearing loses all order. One who is to enter the hells takes the mountain of knives and the forest of swords for a beautiful garden. One who is to fall among animals takes the mare’s womb and the donkey’s foetus for a splendid hall. Even one who has done good and is to be reborn in the human path or the heavenly path cannot escape, at the moment of entering the womb, loving the mother and hating the father, and so receiving a male body, or loving the father and hating the mother, and so receiving a female body. Even a lesser sage of the first fruit, or a bodhisattva at the first arousal of resolve, still has the delusion of the intervening shadow, and cannot enter or leave the womb with right knowledge. All of this is confusion. Because of this confusion at the end of life, they receive rebirth in the seven destinies of the three realms according to their karma.

As the Buddha said: ‘When the mind is pure, the Buddha-land is pure.’ (When the mind is pure, the Buddha-land one is born in is pure as well.) The Buddha also said: ‘All lands are upheld by thought alone.’ (
All lands exist solely upheld by the mind’s thought. As it is said, ‘When the mind arises, all dharmas arise’

) Therefore, when the pure thought of one who recites the Buddha’s name is accomplished, he will certainly be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. Of this, there is of course not the slightest doubt.

“Seven destinies”: hells, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, immortals, gods, and asuras. “Destiny” means the direction toward which one tends. “Buddha-land”: the territory taught and transformed by one Buddha; it is divided into pure lands, defiled lands, fruition-lands, and dharma-nature lands.

blocks.text: 4. Yearning for Bliss, Wearying of Sahā

inline.s: “Yearning and wearying”: yearning for the Land of Ultimate Bliss and wearying of the Sahā world. The sufferings of Sahā are beyond all telling; the bliss of the Land of Ultimate Bliss is beyond all comparison. (For details, see
Yearning for the Land of Ultimate Bliss, Wearying of the Sahā World
“Exhortation”: to admonish and make clear. “Encouragement”: to urge and spur one onward.

“People of the world all contend for matters that are not urgent; amid this fierce evil and extreme suffering they labor body and mind in their business, to support themselves. High and low, rich and poor, young and old, men and women, heap up thoughts and pile up cares, driven on by their minds. Those without fields worry over fields; those without houses worry over houses; for family and wealth, those who have and those who have not worry alike.”

People of the world all contend for vulgar matters that are not urgent; amid this fierce evil and extreme suffering they toil and manage, to support themselves. High and low, rich and poor, young and old, men and women, all heap up thoughts and accumulate cares, scheming and calculating, driven on by their deluded minds. Those without fields worry over fields; those without houses worry over houses; for family and wealth, those who have and those who have not all worry alike (those who have not long to have; those who have fear loss, and long for more).

“Matters that are not urgent”: to be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, to end birth-and-death and escape rebirth — this is the most important matter of all in a human life, and this alone is the urgent business. The vulgar affairs of the world are all matters that are not urgent. “People of the world all contend for matters that are not urgent”: people of the world all vie to busy themselves with trivial vulgar affairs and pay no heed to the pressing great matter before them. They do not know how swiftly impermanence comes, or how great is the matter of birth-and-death, and they spend all their energy and time on vulgar affairs. They only crave fame and gain, with ten thousand worries and sorrows, and the result is that the six paths of rebirth have no end.
Everyone who recites the Buddha’s name knows that
“contending for matters that are not urgent”
is foolish; but those who can truly taste its real meaning and then take action are few. The remedy is:
habitual permeation.

Habitual permeation means wisdom permeating delusion, so that the element of wisdom gradually increases and the element of delusion gradually decreases. When wisdom becomes the master, then where to go and what to do is in one’s own hands (before this it was karmic force that was master), and the obstacles and difficulties in one’s study and practice are solved as they arise. Therefore, habitual permeation is a most important part of study and practice.

Time passes swiftly, and human life is impermanent. Everyone who recites the Buddha’s name must be vigilant at all times, and never take things lightly, frittering away the hours until regret is without end. Bodhisattva Samantabhadra’s Verse to Warn the Assembly says:
“This day has passed, and with it life has dwindled, like a fish in scant water — what
(what)
joy is there in this? Great assembly: you should strive with diligence, as though to put out a fire on your head! Only think on impermanence
(only think on the coming of death)
, and never be self-indulgent
(never give way to indulgence and pleasure)
“A fish in scant water”: a fish in a pond whose waters are daily drying up.
“You should strive with diligence, as though to put out a fire on your head”:
a great fire is blazing on your head and death is swiftly pressing near; reciting the Buddha’s name should be
diligent and unremitting,
quickly
and
without a moment’s delay, seizing the time before unconsciousness and death to accomplish the ten continuous thoughts, so that the habit becomes one’s nature (for details, see
The Condition for Rebirth

). “Impermanence”: having no permanence (all dharmas of the world arise and cease, shift and flow, and do not abide for a single moment); it also means death, or the ghost that snatches away the soul. “Never be self-indulgent”: never give way to indulgence and pleasure, wasting your spirit and your time. The Buddha said:
“Though you labor and suffer for one lifetime, in a mere instant you will afterward be born in the Land of Immeasurable Life, with bliss without end.”
(The Sutra of Immeasurable Life Spoken by the Buddha, Han translation)
“At death all is cast aside, and none follows after”: nothing whatsoever can be taken along; only karma follows the body. Once impermanence arrives, then one knows oneself to be a person in a dream.

“Having one, one lacks another, and longs to be equal to the rest. When one has just a little, one worries again over the impermanent. Water and fire, thieves and robbers, enemies and creditors, burn, drown, plunder, and seize, scattering and obliterating all. The mind is stingy, the will stubborn, and one cannot let go. At death all is cast away, and none follows after. Rich and poor alike — ten thousand worries and sorrows.”

Having one thing, one feels the lack of another, and compares oneself endlessly (longing to be equal to the rest), for the gully of desire is hard to fill. When one has just a little, one worries again that worldly things are impermanent, and that all one possesses will be flooded, burned, robbed, trampled, or plundered by water and fire, by thieves and robbers, by enemies (including prodigal sons) and creditors, and so scattered and obliterated. The mind is stingy and stubborn, and one cannot let go. Yet at the end of life it must all be left behind, and not one thing can be carried away. Rich and poor are both like this, with ten thousand worries and sorrows.

“People of the world — fathers and sons, brothers, husbands and wives, kin and relatives — should respect and love one another, and not hate or envy one another. They should share what they have and supply what they lack, and not be greedy or stingy. Their speech and countenance should always be gentle, and they should not oppose or contradict one another. If at times their minds contend and anger arises, in later lives it grows ever fiercer, until it becomes a great enmity. In the affairs of the world, people bring harm upon one another; though the fruit does not appear at once, one should urgently break through this and understand it.”

People of the world — fathers and sons, brothers, husbands and wives, kin and relatives — should respect and love one another, and not hate or envy one another. They should help one another, sharing what they have and supplying what they lack, and must not be greedy or stingy. They should speak gently and lovingly, and not contradict or mock one another. If for a time they go against one another and a contentious mind arises, with some resentment and strife, in later lives it grows worse by turns, until at last it becomes a great enmity (these four lines say that in the world people often cannot bear a small matter, and so it becomes a great enmity, a great hatred, even to the ruin of the family and the loss of life). In the affairs of the world, people bring harm upon one another; though the evil fruit does not appear at that moment (though it does not come at once), the evil cause has already been made, and where there is a cause there must be a fruit. One should at once break through and understand the cause and effect between them, and not rashly create it (these lines say that one should be a clear-headed person regarding cause and effect. Ordinary beings know only to fear the fruit; bodhisattvas know to fear the cause).

“People caught in love and desire are born alone and die alone, go alone and come alone; their suffering and joy they bear themselves, and none can take their place. Their good and evil change and transform, following upon where they are born; their roads differ, and the time of meeting is not fixed. Why not, while strong and healthy, strive to cultivate goodness? What are you waiting for?”

People are sunk in love and desire, not understanding that in truth they are born alone and die alone, go alone and come alone, bearing their own suffering and joy, with no one to take their place. Each one’s good and evil change and transform, and fruit follows upon cause; since causes and fruits differ, their roads after death differ too, and the time of meeting again is not fixed. Why not, while strong and healthy, strive to cultivate goodness? What are you waiting for?

“People of the world cannot see their own good and evil, yet each vies to bring about his own fortune or misfortune, calamity or blessing. Body foolish and spirit dim, they pass on and receive other teachings; their inverted views continue without cease — this is the root of impermanence. Dull and benighted, they rush against things and do not believe in the scriptures and the Dharma. Their minds take no far thought, and each seeks only his own pleasure. Deluded by anger, greedy for wealth and lust, they never stop. How pitiful and sad!”

People of the world are deluded, unable to see their own good and evil, not understanding the cause and effect of fortune and misfortune, calamity and blessing; they seek only the pleasure of the moment and vie with one another in creating karma (knowing nothing of the cause, they do not fear the fruit). Body foolish and spirit dim (their conduct foolish, their minds benighted), such inverted views are passed on and taught from one to another (one need only look at the films, news, and arts of today, filled with killing, stealing, and lust, and with greed, anger, and delusion, which steep children, young people, and adults through eye and ear alike, to know how “inverted views are passed on and taught”). Their inverted and perverse conduct continues without cease — this is the root of birth-and-death and rebirth. Dull and benighted (childish and ignorant of reason), they rush against things, and do not believe in the scriptures and the Dharma. Their minds take no far thought, and each seeks only the pleasure of the moment. Deluded by anger, greedy for wealth and lust, they never stop. How pitiful and sad!

“Their forebears were not good, and did not know the Way and its virtue; there was no one to tell them, so it is no wonder at all. The destinies of death and birth, the paths of good and evil — they believe in none of them, and say no such thing exists. But look at one another, and you will see it for yourselves.”

Their forebears were not good (both foolish and evil), and did not know the Way and its virtue; therefore no one rightly taught them, and so it is no wonder that their conduct was foolish and their minds benighted. The destinies of death and birth, the six paths of good and evil — they believe in none of them, and say no such thing exists. But only observe carefully, and you will see it for yourselves.

“Sometimes a father weeps for a son, sometimes a son weeps for a father; brothers, husbands and wives weep for one another by turns. One dies, one is born; again and again they look back in longing. Bound by sorrow and love, they have no time of release. Thinking ever on kindness and affection, they never leave desire behind. They cannot think deeply or plan carefully, or single-mindedly and intently walk the Way. The years and the lifespan swiftly end, and there is nothing to be done!”

Sometimes a son dies and the father weeps, or a father dies and the son weeps; brothers, husbands and wives weep for one another. One dies, one is born, and they cannot bear to part. Bound by sorrow and love, they have no time of release. They think only of kindness and affection and fondness, never leaving desire behind. Yet they cannot think deeply or plan carefully, or single-mindedly and intently walk the Way. The lifespan is gone in a flash, and there is nothing to be done!

“Many are those deluded about the Way, few are those who awaken to it. Each harbors a heart of killing and venom, and evil airs hang dark. For the sake of delusion they stir up trouble, opposing Heaven and Earth. Giving free rein to their will, their evil reaches its extreme; their lifespan is suddenly snatched away. They fall into the evil paths, with no end in sight.”

Many are those deluded about the Way, few are those who awaken to it. Each harbors a heart of killing (destroying the other) and venom (malice), and evil airs spread far. They stir up trouble and do evil, opposing Heaven and Earth. Giving free rein to their will, their evil reaches its extreme (their wickedness is full to overflowing); their lifespan is suddenly snatched away, and they fall into the evil paths, with no end in sight.

“You should think deeply and plan carefully, keep far from all evil, and choose what is good, diligently putting it into practice. Love and desire, glory and splendor cannot be kept forever; all must be parted from, and there is no joy in them. You should strive with diligence and be born in the Land of Peace and Bliss. There your wisdom will be bright and penetrating, and your merit and virtue surpassing. Do not follow the desires of your own heart, failing the scriptures and the precepts, and falling behind others.”

You should think deeply and plan carefully, keep far from all evil, and choose what is good, diligently putting it into practice. Love and desire, glory and splendor cannot be kept forever; all must be parted from, and there is no joy in them. You should be diligent and strive, seeking rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. Once there, your wisdom will be bright and penetrating, and your merit and virtue surpassing. You must never follow the desires of your own heart, failing the scriptures and the precepts, and falling behind others.

“You”: you all. “You should strive with diligence and be born in the Land of Peace and Bliss”: though you strive with diligence and labor and suffer for one lifetime, it is but a moment; afterward you are born in the Land of Immeasurable Life, with bliss without end.

“Maitreya spoke: The Buddha’s words of teaching and admonition are most profound and most good. We have all received your compassionate grace and are freed from sorrow and suffering. The Buddha is the King of the Dharma, honored above all sages; his radiance shines through all, penetrating to the boundless, and he is the teacher of all gods and humans. Now we have met the Buddha and again heard the sound of Immeasurable Life; there is none who does not rejoice, and our minds attain clarity.”

Bodhisattva Maitreya addressed the World-Honored One: The Buddha’s words of teaching and admonition are most profound and most good. We have all received the Buddha’s compassionate grace and are freed from sorrow and suffering. The Buddha is the King of the Dharma, honored above all sages; his radiance shines through all, penetrating to the boundless, and he is the teacher of all gods and humans. Today we have received the Buddha’s teaching and admonition, and again heard the name of Amitābha Buddha (how important this is! If one does not even know the name of Amitābha Buddha, how could one be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss and end birth-and-death and escape rebirth?); there is none who does not rejoice, and our minds attain clarity.
“Again heard the sound of Immeasurable Life”:
again hearing the name of Amitābha Buddha.
For the note on how “the sound of Immeasurable Life” is “the name of Amitābha Buddha,” see the line “If there are sentient beings who hear the Buddha’s sound” in “45. This Sutra Alone Will Remain.”

“The Buddha told Maitreya: To revere the Buddha is the greatest goodness. You should truly recite the Buddha’s name, cut off the fox-like doubt, uproot all love and desire, and stop up the source of every evil. Then you may walk freely through the three realms without any hindrance, reveal the right Way, and deliver those not yet delivered.”

The Buddha told Bodhisattva Maitreya: To revere the Buddha is the greatest goodness. You should truly recite the Buddha’s name, cut off the fox-like doubt, uproot all love and desire, and stop up (block) the source of every evil. Once reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, you may walk freely through the three realms without any hindrance, reveal the right Way, and deliver those not yet delivered.

“You should truly recite the Buddha’s name, and cut off fox-like doubt”: the fox is by nature full of doubt, and so a mind that wavers in doubt is called “fox-like doubt.” The root cause of a practitioner’s dread of difficulty and his sloth is that he half believes and half doubts the Pure Land scriptures and commentaries and the teachings of the patriarchs (believing some, doubting some; or believing for a while, then not believing for a while). If his faith is true and his vow earnest, he will certainly follow the scriptures and commentaries and the patriarchs’ teachings, practicing as they say, and press boldly forward:
thought after thought continuous, with the end of life as the term; steeling the mind and subduing the self, never ceasing day or night
(for details, see
Master Shandao’s Three Teachings
— This is the path of “ten thoughts, ten rebirths; a hundred thoughts, a hundred rebirths” opened for us by Master Shandao, who was Amitābha Buddha come again.

“You should know that the people of the ten directions, from kalpa to kalpa without beginning, have turned and turned through the five paths, their sorrow and suffering unbroken. At birth there is pain, in old age pain, in grave illness pain, and at death pain. Foul and impure, there is nothing to delight in. You should resolve for yourselves, wash away the stains of the mind, and make your words and deeds loyal and true, so that within and without correspond.”

You should know that the people of the ten directions, since kalpas without beginning, have turned and turned through the five paths (gods, humans, hells, hungry ghosts, and animals), their sorrow and suffering unbroken. At birth there is pain, in old age pain, in grave illness pain, and at death pain. Foul and impure, there is nothing to delight in. You should make your resolve, cut off the evil cause, wash away the stains of the mind, and make your words and deeds loyal and true, so that within and without correspond.

“People can save themselves, and in turn rescue one another. With the utmost sincerity seek your vow and accumulate the roots of goodness. Though you strive with diligence and labor and suffer for one lifetime, it is but a moment; afterward you are born in the Land of Immeasurable Life, with bliss without end. You will forever uproot the source of birth-and-death, and no longer suffer the affliction of sorrow. Your life will be a thousand, ten thousand kalpas, at ease and as you wish.”

People can save themselves, and only then can they save others; thus turning and turning, they rescue one another. You should with the utmost sincerity seek the vow of rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, and accumulate the roots of goodness. Though you strive with diligence and labor and suffer for one lifetime, it is but a moment; afterward you are born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, with bliss without end. You will forever uproot the source of birth-and-death, and no longer suffer the affliction of sorrow. Your life will be a thousand, ten thousand kalpas, at ease and as you wish.

“Roots of goodness”: roots of goodness, goodness. Because goodness is the cause of bodhi, it is called the root of goodness, the root of good. “Accumulate the roots of goodness” means single-mindedly and constantly reciting the name of Amitābha Buddha. Because holding the name and reciting the Buddha is precisely the root of goodness for rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, “accumulate the roots of goodness” here means single-mindedly and constantly reciting the name of Amitābha Buddha.
“Each should strive with diligence, and seek what his heart desires. Do not doubt or regret, and bring fault
(jiù)
upon yourself, and be born in the seven-treasure city of the border land, there to endure every hardship for five hundred years.”

You must each strive with diligence, and seek what your heart desires — rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. Do not doubt or regret, and bring fault upon yourself, and be born in the seven-treasure city of the border land, there to endure every hardship for five hundred years.
“Fault” (jiù): a transgression; an error. “The seven-treasure city of the border land”: for details, see “40. The Border Land and the City of Doubt” below.
“Maitreya spoke: Having received the Buddha’s clear instruction, we will single-mindedly and intently study and practice, doing as taught, and dare not doubt.”

Bodhisattva Maitreya addressed the World-Honored One: Having received the Buddha’s clear instruction, we will certainly single-mindedly and intently study and practice, doing as taught, and dare not doubt.

blocks.text: 35. The Evil Suffering of the Turbid World

inline.s: The evil suffering of the turbid world: the five evils, the five pains, and the five burnings. The five evils are the karmic cause; the five pains and the five burnings are the karmic retribution. Within the retribution: the five pains are the flower-retribution; the five burnings are the fruit-retribution.

“The Buddha told Maitreya: That you can in this world rectify your minds and set your intentions aright, and do no evil, is a great virtue. Why is that? In the worlds of the ten directions there is much good and little evil, and they are easy to teach and transform. Only this world of the five evils is the most bitterly suffering. I now become a Buddha here to teach and transform the multitudes of beings, causing them to abandon the five evils, leave behind the five pains, and escape the five burnings, subduing and transforming their minds, causing them to keep the five goods and obtain their merit and blessing.”

The Buddha told Bodhisattva Maitreya: That you can in this world rectify your minds and set your intentions aright, and do no evil, is a great virtue beyond the ordinary. Why is that? In the worlds of the ten directions there is much good and little evil, and they are easy to teach and transform. Only this world of the five evils is the most bitterly suffering. I now become a Buddha here to teach and transform living beings, causing them to abandon the five evils, leave behind the five pains, and escape the five burnings, subduing and transforming their minds of evildoing, causing them to keep the five goods and obtain merit and blessing.

“The five evils, the five pains, and the five burnings”: killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, and drinking alcohol — these are the five evils. One who commits these five evils, in this present life, is like a criminal punished by law and suffers calamity in his person: this is called the five pains. Because of these five evils, in future lives he falls into the three evil paths and receives retribution: this is called the five burnings. The five evils are the karmic cause; the five pains and the five burnings are the karmic retribution. Within the retribution: the five pains are the flower-retribution; the five burnings are the fruit-retribution. “Karmic cause”: the cause of retribution for good and evil. Good karma is the cause of blissful fruit; evil karma is the cause of suffering fruit. “Flower-retribution”: also written “hua-retribution.” The flower opens before the fruit is borne, and so “flower-retribution” is spoken in contrast to the “fruit-retribution” obtained afterward. For example, a man plants a tree in order to obtain its fruit; besides obtaining the fruit itself, he also obtains flowers — this is the flower-retribution. When sentient beings plant the karmic causes of good and evil, the fruit they thereby obtain is the fruit-retribution, and what they obtain besides, before the fruit-retribution, is called the flower-retribution. “The five goods”: namely the five precepts — not killing, not stealing, not committing sexual misconduct, not speaking falsely, and not drinking alcohol.
“Not drinking alcohol”: not drinking or inhaling alcoholic liquors or drugs that stupefy human nature.

“Merit and blessing”: the blessed retribution evoked by practicing the good conduct of humans and gods. Merit and blessing differ from merit and virtue: outward practice of worldly works, being outflows-laden good, is “merit and blessing”; inward realization of the Buddha-nature, being outflow-free good, is “merit and virtue.” Again, cultivating the Way with attachment to marks is “merit and blessing”; cultivating the Way free of marks is “merit and virtue.” Hence in the bodhisattva’s practice “no-marks” is often spoken of, and no-marks means to be free of marks even amid marks. (For details, see
The Practice of the Three Non’s: No-Thought, No-Mark, No-Abiding
) “Outflows”: outflow is another name for affliction; having outflows means having affliction, and being free of outflows means being free of affliction.

“What are the five? The first: the various kinds of sentient beings in the world wish to do every evil. The strong overpower the weak, and in turn plunder and prey on one another, maiming, harming, wounding, and killing, devouring one another in turn
(dàn — that is, to eat)
. Not knowing to do good, they afterward suffer calamity and punishment; hence there are the poor and beggars, the orphaned and solitary, the deaf and blind
and the mute
(yīn,
unable to speak
the dumb,
the foolish and wicked, the deformed
wāng

and the mad. All this is because in former lives they did not believe in the Way and its virtue and would not do good. As for those who are noble and wealthy, wise and eminent elders, brave in wisdom and accomplished in talent, all this comes from compassion and filial piety in former lives, from cultivating good and accumulating virtue.”

What are the five? The first: the various kinds of sentient beings in the world wish to do every evil. The strong bully the weak, and in turn bring harm and venom upon one another (plunder and prey), maiming, harming, wounding, and killing, swallowing one another in turn. Not knowing to do good, they afterward suffer calamity and punishment; hence there are the poor and miserable, the beggars, the orphaned and the widowed, the deaf and the blind, the mute and the foolish, the deformed and the mad. All this is because in former lives they did not believe in the Way and its virtue and would not do good. As for those who are noble and wealthy, wise and eminent elders, brave in wisdom and accomplished in talent, all this comes from compassion, loyalty, and filial piety in former lives, from cultivating good and accumulating virtue.
“Widowers and widows” (guān): widowers (men without wives) and widows. “The deformed” (wāng): a crooked and misshapen frame; it also means one who has such a deformity.

“In the world there are these things, present before your eyes. After the end of life, one enters the dark realm, is reborn and receives a body, changes form and alters path. Hence there are the hells (niraya), the birds and beasts, and the creeping and crawling kinds. It is like the prisons of worldly law, with bitter suffering and extreme punishment: the soul and spirit, the vital essence, follow their offenses whither they tend. The lifespan they receive is long or short; they follow one another and are born together, repaying one another in turn. Until the calamity and evil are exhausted, they can never leave. Turning and turning within it, for many kalpas they find it hard to escape. Deliverance is hard to obtain, and the pain is beyond words. Between Heaven and Earth this is naturally so. Though the retribution does not come at once, good and evil will surely return to their doer.”

One who commits these evils, while alive in the world, has these retributions present before his eyes. After his life ends, he enters the dark realm, is reborn and receives a body, changes form (casting off the human body) and alters path (falling into the evil paths). Hence there are the hells (niraya), the birds and beasts, and the creeping and crawling kinds. It is like the prisons of worldly law, with bitter suffering and extreme punishment: the consciousness (soul and spirit, vital essence) is punished according to the weight of its offenses. The lifespan received is long or short; enemies and foes are born together and repay one another in turn (enmity repaid with enmity, without end). Until the calamity and evil are exhausted, they can never leave the evil paths. Turning and turning within it, for many kalpas they find it hard to escape. Deliverance is hard to obtain, and the pain is beyond words. Between Heaven and Earth this law of cause and effect is naturally so. Even if retribution does not come at once, the repayment of good and evil will at last be fulfilled.

“Niraya”: a transliteration of Sanskrit; translated, “hell.” “It is like the prisons of worldly law, with bitter suffering and extreme punishment”: it is like the king’s law punishing a criminal — first he is shut into prison, his body bound in chains, beaten and interrogated; this figures the flower-retribution in the present body. At the last he is put to the extreme punishment and his life cut off; this figures the fruit-retribution after death.

“The second: the people of the world do not follow the laws and institutions, but are extravagant, lewd, arrogant, and self-indulgent, giving their minds free rein. Those above are not clear-minded, those in office are not upright; they entrap people in injustice and harm the loyal and good. Their hearts and mouths differ, and their scheming and falsehood are manifold. High and low, kin and stranger, all cheat one another. Angry and deluded, they wish to enrich themselves and crave to have much. In profit and loss, victory and defeat, they knot up resentment into enmity, ruin their families and lose their lives, giving no thought to what comes before or after. The rich are stingy and will not give. Their love of possession is deep and their greed heavy; their minds toil and their bodies suffer. So it goes to the very end, and not one thing follows them. Good and evil, calamity and blessing, pursue the life where one is born: one may go to a place of bliss, or enter into bitter poison.”

The second: the people of the world do not follow the laws and institutions, but are extravagant, lewd, arrogant, and self-indulgent, giving their minds free rein and seeking only their own pleasure. Those above are not clear-minded, those in office are not upright; they entrap people in injustice and harm the loyal and good. Their hearts and mouths differ (speaking of benevolence, righteousness, and morality, while in their hearts are killing, stealing, lust, and falsehood), and their scheming and falsehood are manifold. High and low, kin and stranger, all cheat one another. Angry and deluded, they wish to enrich themselves (thinking only of their own advantage) and crave to have much (thinking only of having more themselves). In their deceits and strifes, in profit and loss, victory and defeat, they knot up resentment into enmity, ruin their families and lose their lives, giving no thought to what comes before or after. Though rich, they are stingy by nature and will not give. Their love and clinging are firm and their greed is deep; their minds toil and their bodies suffer. So at the end of life, not one thing follows them (not one thing can be carried away). The blessing of good causes and the calamity of evil causes follow the world into which they are born. One may go to a place of bliss, or enter into bitter poison.

“Again, some see the good and hate and slander them, never thinking to admire or emulate them. They constantly harbor a thievish mind, coveting others’ profit to supply themselves, squandering it and then taking more. The gods record it all, and in the end they enter the evil paths. Of themselves there are the three paths, with immeasurable suffering; turning and turning within them, for many kalpas they find it hard to escape, and the pain is beyond words.”

Again, some see the good and hate and slander them, never thinking to revere or emulate them. They constantly harbor a thievish mind, scheming after others’ profit to supply themselves, squandering it and then seizing more. The gods record it all in their ledgers, and at the end of life they enter the evil paths. Of themselves there are the three paths, with immeasurable suffering; turning and turning within them, for many kalpas they find it hard to escape, and the pain is beyond words.
“To covet” (xī): to long for. “The gods record it all, and in the end they enter the evil paths”: good and evil at the last are always repaid; three feet above your head the gods are watching.

“The third: the people of the world, born one from another’s causes, how long is their lifespan? The unwholesome, whose bodies and minds are not upright, constantly harbor evil and think of lewdness. Their breasts are full of fretfulness, and their lewd ways show outwardly. They waste and damage their family wealth and do what is unlawful. What they ought to seek, they refuse to do.”

The third: the people of the world, born one from another’s causes (all lodging here through the karmic causes they have made), how long is their lifespan (how long can they live)? The unwholesome, whose bodies and minds are not upright, constantly harbor evil, lewd and unrestrained. Their breasts are full of fretfulness, and their lewd ways show outwardly. (Their lewd conduct) wastes and damages their family wealth and does what is unlawful. What they ought to seek, they refuse to do.
“Yì” (
yì
): wantonness.

“Again, some band together and gather in companies, raise troops and war on one another. They attack, plunder, and slaughter; they seize by force and threaten, and bring it all home to wives and children, giving themselves up to pleasure. All alike detest and weary of them, and suffer from their harm. Such evil as this is manifest to humans and ghosts. The gods record it, and of themselves they enter the three paths. With immeasurable suffering, turning and turning within them, for many kalpas they find it hard to escape, and the pain is beyond words.”

Again, some band together and gather in companies, raise troops and war on one another. They attack, plunder, and slaughter; they seize by force and threaten, and (the goods thus robbed and plundered) bring them home to wives and children, giving themselves up to pleasure. All alike detest and weary of them, and suffer from their harm. Such evil as this is manifest to humans and ghosts. The gods record it in their ledgers, and of themselves they fall into the three paths (the three evil paths). With immeasurable suffering, turning and turning within them, for many kalpas they find it hard to escape, and the pain is beyond words.

“The fourth: the people of the world do not think to cultivate goodness. They are double-tongued, foul-mouthed, lying, and given to idle talk. They hate and envy the good, and ruin the wise and eminent. They are unfilial to their parents and slight their teachers and elders. With friends they have no faith, and are seldom honest. Proud and self-important, they claim to have the Way. They run riot with power and might, and insult and despise others. They wish to be feared and revered, and feel no shame or dread. They are hard to subdue and transform, and constantly harbor arrogance.”

The fourth: the people of the world do not think to cultivate goodness. They are double-tongued, foul-mouthed, lying, and given to idle talk. They hate and envy the good and attack and slander the wise and eminent. They are unfilial to their parents and slight their teachers and elders. With friends they have no faith, and are seldom honest. Proud and self-important, they claim to have the Way. They run riot and bully, using their power to oppress others. They wish to be feared and revered, and are not ashamed or contrite. They are hard to teach and subdue, and constantly harbor arrogance.

“By reliance on the merit and blessing of former lives, they are sheltered and protected; now in this life they do evil, and that merit and blessing is utterly destroyed. When the lifespan at last ends, all evils gather round them. Moreover, their names are enrolled and recorded by the gods. Their calamity and guilt draw them on, and there is no way to escape. They can only go forward into the cauldron of fire. Body and mind are shattered, and spirit and form suffer to the utmost. At such a time, what use is regret?”

The reason they are human in this life is that they relied on the merit and blessing of former lives for shelter and protection; but doing evil in this life, that merit and blessing is utterly destroyed. When the lifespan at last ends, all evils gather round them. Moreover, all they have done is recorded by the gods, one by one. Once the life ends, their calamity and guilt (evil karma) draw them on, and there is no way to leave the evil paths. The consciousness can only go forward into the cauldron and boiling vat of hell. Body and mind are shattered, and spirit and form suffer to the utmost. When that time comes, regret is too late!
“Huò” (
huò
): a great cauldron, often used as the instrument for boiling men alive. “Cauldron and vat”: the cruel punishment of casting a man into a cauldron of boiling water and boiling him to death.

“The fifth: the people of the world are indolent and idle, unwilling to do good or to discipline body and mind and cultivate their work. They oppose and defy their parents’ teachings. They are like enemies; better to have had no children. They betray grace and turn from righteousness, and make no repayment. They give themselves up to roaming and scattering, steeped in wine and greedy of delicacies. Rude and overbearing
hù

they rush against others, knowing nothing of human decency. Without righteousness or propriety, they cannot be admonished or made to understand. For the six close kin and their households, whether they have what they need, they cannot bring themselves to care.”

The fifth: the people of the world are sunk in pleasure and idleness (indolent), slothful and lazy, unwilling to do good or to discipline body and mind and cultivate right work. To their parents’ teachings they are contrary (opposing) and rebellious, like enemies and foes — such children are better not had. They betray grace and turn from righteousness toward their parents, and make no repayment. They give themselves up to pleasure and roaming, steeped in wine (drinking to excess) and greedy of delicacies (craving fine food). Rude (boorish) and overbearing (hù) and contrary (defiant), they do not understand the way of being human (human decency). Without righteousness or propriety, they cannot be admonished (corrected) or made to understand (enlightened). For the six close kin (father, mother, elder and younger brothers, wife, children) and their households, whether they have the necessities of life (what is needed to sustain life) or not, they are wholly unconcerned.
“Loitering”: lingering without purpose. “Overbearing” (
hù
): despotic and violent.

“They do not think on the grace of their parents, nor keep the righteousness of teacher and friend. In intention, thought, body, and speech there is not one good thing. They do not believe in the scriptures and Dharmas of the Buddhas, nor in birth-and-death and good and evil. They wish to harm the true persons and to throw the assembly of monks into confusion. Deluded and benighted, they take themselves for wise. They do not know whence they have come in birth, or whither they go in death. Unkind and unfilial, they hope for long life. Though taught with a compassionate heart, they will not believe. Though spoken to with bitter words, it profits them nothing. Their minds are stopped up, and their understanding does not open. When the great life is about to end, regret and fear come together. Not having cultivated good beforehand, they repent only at the last. But repenting afterward — what use will it be?”

They do not think on the grace of their parents, nor keep in heart the righteousness of teacher and friend. In intention, thought, action, and speech, they have never had a single good. They do not believe in the scriptures and Dharmas of the Buddhas, nor in birth-and-death and the retribution of good and evil. They wish to entrap true persons who have attained the fruit, and to throw the assembly of monks into confusion (to break the harmonious Sangha). Deluded and benighted, they take themselves for wise. They do not know whence they have come in birth, or whither they go in death. Unkind and unfilial, they hope for long life. Though taught with a compassionate heart, they will not believe. Though admonished with bitter words, it profits them nothing. Their minds are stopped up, and their understanding does not open. When the great life is about to end, regret and fear come together. Not having cultivated good beforehand, they repent and fear only at the last. Repenting and fearing at that point — what use is it?

“Between Heaven and Earth the five paths are clearly distinguished. The retribution of good and evil, calamity and blessing following upon one another, each bears himself, and no one takes his place. When the good do good, they pass from joy to joy, from light to light. When the evil do evil, they pass from suffering to suffering, from darkness to darkness. Who can know this? Only the Buddha knows.”

Between Heaven and Earth the five paths (gods, humans, hells, hungry ghosts, and animals) are clearly distinguished. The retribution of good and evil, calamity and blessing following upon one another, each bears himself, and no one takes his place. When the good do good, they pass from joy to joy, from light to light. When the evil do evil, they pass from suffering to suffering, from darkness to darkness. Who can know the reason of it? Only the Buddha knows.

“Though the Buddha teaches and instructs, those who believe and practice are few. Birth-and-death does not cease, and the evil paths are not emptied. The people of the world are such that they cannot be fully told. Hence there are the three paths of nature, with immeasurable suffering, and they turn and turn within them. Life after life, kalpa upon kalpa, there is no end in sight. Deliverance is hard to obtain, and the pain is beyond words.”

The Buddha teaches and instructs, but those who believe and practice are few. Therefore their birth-and-death and rebirth does not cease, and their falling into the evil paths is unbroken. Such people of the world cannot be fully told of. Hence of nature there are the three evil paths, with immeasurable suffering, and they turn and turn within them. Life after life, kalpa upon kalpa, there is no end in sight. Deliverance is hard to obtain, and the pain is beyond words.

“Such are the five evils, five pains, and five burnings: they are like a great fire burning the human body. If one can, amid them, single-mindedly master one’s mind, rectify the body and set up right mindfulness; if one’s words match one’s deeds, and all one does is utterly sincere; if one alone does every good and does no evil — then one’s own body is delivered, one obtains that merit and blessing, and may gain long life and the Way of nirvāṇa. This is what is called the five great goods!”

Such are the five evils, five pains, and five burnings: they are like a great fire burning the human body. If one can, amid them, single-mindedly master one’s mind (steel the mind and subdue the self), rectify the body and set up right mindfulness; if one’s words match one’s deeds, and all one does is utterly sincere; if one alone does every good and does no evil — then one’s body is delivered, one obtains that merit and blessing, and may gain long life and the Way of nirvāṇa. This is what is called the five great goods!
“To match”: to correspond; to accord. “Alone doing every good and doing no evil”: the Verse of the Seven Buddhas’ Common Precepts says:
“Do no evil; practice all good; purify your own mind — this is the teaching of all Buddhas
(this is the admonition of all Buddhas)

“The Buddha told Maitreya: I say to you all, these five evils, five pains, and five burnings give rise to one another in turn. Whoever dares to transgress them shall pass through the evil destinies. Perhaps in this present life he is first visited by sickness and calamity, unable to die and unable to live, made an example for all to see. Or at the end of his lifespan he enters the three evil paths, where sorrow and pain, cruel and poisonous, of themselves scorch
jiāo
him in the fires of hell.”

The Buddha told Bodhisattva Maitreya: I say to you all, these five evils, five pains, and five burnings give rise to one another in turn. Whoever dares to transgress them shall pass through the evil destinies. In this present life he is first visited by sickness and suffering (the flower-retribution), unable to live and unable to die (unable to seek life, unable to seek death), so that the multitude may see it and know that cause and effect are not empty. When his life ends, he falls into the three evil paths (the fruit-retribution), where sorrow and pain, cruel and poisonous, and the fires of hell scorch him through his own karma.
“Or”: there is. “Cruel and poisonous”: the most miserable of punishments. “Of themselves scorched (
jiāo
) and burned”: by one’s own karma one is visited by the blazing fire of hell. The Hui Commentary says:
“Scorched and burned describes the fierceness of the hell-fire. ‘Of themselves’ means that it is evoked by one’s own karma.”

“With their enemies they wound and kill one another in turn. From a tiny beginning it becomes a great disaster. All this is because they greedily cling to wealth and lust, and will not bestow kindness. Each wishes only his own pleasure, and no longer cares for right and wrong. Driven by deluded desire, they enrich themselves and strive for profit; wealth and honor, glory and splendor, are the pleasure of the moment. They cannot endure insult, and take no pains to cultivate good. Their power and might last but a little while, and are soon worn away. The Way of Heaven spreads its net, and of itself gathers
(in ancient usage, the same as “to correct”)
and seizes them. Lonely
qióng
and frightened
sōng
they must enter into it. From ancient times to now this has been so — how painful, how sad!”

With their enemies and foes, they wound and kill one another without cease. From a tiny dispute it becomes a great disaster. All this is because they greedily cling to wealth and lust, and will not bestow kindness. Each wishes only his own pleasure, and no longer cares for right and wrong. Driven by deluded desire, they enrich themselves and strive for profit; wealth and honor, glory and splendor, are the pleasure of the moment. They cannot endure insult, and take no pains to cultivate good. Their power and might last but a little while, and are soon worn away. The Way of Heaven spreads its net, and of itself corrects and exposes them; their own consciousness, lonely and terrified (lone and fearful), falls into the evil paths. From ancient times to now this has been so — how painful, how sad!
“Spreads its net”: to put into effect. “Lonely (
qióng
) and alone”: the appearance of being desolate. “Frightened (
sōng
) and fearful”: the appearance of alarm and unrest.

“You who have obtained the Buddha’s words from the scriptures should ponder them deeply, each holding to them uprightly, never slackening to the end of your lives. Revere the sages, honor the good, be kind and compassionate and broadly loving. You should seek to cross over the world, and to uproot and cut off the source of the many evils of birth-and-death. You should leave the three paths, the road of sorrow, dread, and pain.”

You who have been fortunate to obtain the Buddha’s teachings should ponder them over and over and deeply, each holding to them uprightly, never slackening to the end of your lives. Revere the sages, honor the good, be kind and compassionate and broadly loving. Save yourselves and save others, and uproot and cut off the source of the many evils of birth-and-death. You should leave the three paths (hells, hungry ghosts, and animals), the road of sorrow, dread, and pain.

“When you do good, what is first? You should rectify your own mind, rectify your own body; ears, eyes, mouth, and nose should all be rectified. With body and mind pure and clean, you accord with good. Do not follow your cravings, and do not transgress against any evil. Your speech and countenance should be gentle, and your bodily conduct single-minded. In every movement and every glance, be calm and at ease, and act deliberately. To act in haste brings failure and regret afterward. To do a thing without care loses all the work you have done.”

When you do good, what comes first? It is to rectify your own mind, to rectify your own body; ears, eyes, mouth, and nose should all be rectified. Cause body and mind to be pure and clean, so that you accord with good. Do not follow your cravings, and do not transgress against any evil. Your speech and countenance should be gentle, and your bodily conduct should be single-minded in walking the Way. In every movement and every glance, be calm and at ease. To act rashly and in haste brings failure and regret afterward. Because of carelessness and lack of scrutiny, all the work you have done is lost.

“You should rectify your own mind, rectify your own body; ears, eyes, mouth, and nose should all be rectified”: think nothing against reason, do nothing against reason, hear nothing against reason, see nothing against reason, speak nothing against reason, smell nothing against reason.
“In every movement and every glance, be calm and at ease”: in every movement, be serene and composed.
“To act in haste”: to act rashly and recklessly, without examining one’s own thoughts and desires.

“Care”: careful. “To do a thing without care loses all the work you have done”: because of carelessness and lack of scrutiny, one loses one’s practice. Therefore, in whatever one undertakes, one should first examine carefully whether it is right or wrong, beneficial or harmful; it must accord with principle, and only then should it be done. This is the awakened mind, different from the wild and confused mind.

blocks.text: 37. Like the Poor Man Who Finds a Treasure

inline.s: “You should widely plant the roots of virtue, and not transgress the prohibitions of the Way. Be patient and forbearing, diligent and advancing, compassionate and single-minded, pure in fasting and precepts. One day and one night here surpasses a hundred years of doing good in the Land of Immeasurable Life. Why is that? In that Buddha-land all is accumulated virtue and every good, without a hair’s breadth of evil. To cultivate good here for ten days and ten nights surpasses a thousand years of doing good in the Buddha-lands of other directions. Why is that? In the Buddha-lands of other directions merit and blessing come of themselves, and there is no place for doing evil. Only in this world is there little good and much evil, drinking bitterness and eating poison, never at rest.”

You should widely plant the roots of virtue, and never transgress the precepts. Be patient and forbearing, diligent and advancing, compassionate and single-minded, pure in fasting and precepts. To do good in this world for one day and one night surpasses a hundred years of doing good in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Why is that? Because in the Land of Ultimate Bliss all is accumulated virtue and every good, without a hair’s breadth of evil. To cultivate good in this world for ten days and ten nights surpasses a thousand years of doing good in the Buddha-lands of other directions. Why is that? Because in the Buddha-lands of other directions merit and blessing come of themselves, and there is no place for doing evil. Only in this world is there little good and much evil, drinking bitterness and eating poison, never ceasing.
“The prohibitions of the Way”: the various evils forbidden by the Buddha-Way, namely the precepts.

“I pity you all, and with toil of heart teach and instruct you, bestowing on you the scriptures and the Dharma. Hold it all in mind and ponder it, and practice it all. High and low, men and women, kin and friends, should teach and exhort one another, and mutually restrain and check themselves. Be harmonious and compliant with principle, joyful and kind and filial. If you do what is transgressive, then repent of your own fault. Leave evil and draw near good; hear it in the morning and change by evening.
Uphold the scriptures and precepts as a poor man who has found a treasure.
Amend the past and cultivate the future; wash
xǐ
the mind and change your conduct. Then blessings will come down in response, and whatever you wish you will
zhé
obtain.”

I pity you all, and with toil of heart teach and instruct you, bestowing on you the scriptures and the Dharma. You must all receive and hold them, ponder them, and practice them. High and low, men and women, kin and friends, must all teach and exhort one another, and mutually restrain and check themselves (rectify your own mind, rectify your own body). Be harmonious and compliant with principle, joyful and kind and filial. If you transgress the precepts, then repent of your own fault. Leave evil and draw near good; hear it in the morning and change by evening. Uphold the scriptures and precepts as a poor man who has found a treasure. Amend the past and cultivate the future (correct the evil done before, and diligently cultivate the good of the present and the future), wash the mind and change your conduct. Then blessings will come down in response, and whatever you seek will be fulfilled.
“Upholding the scriptures and precepts”: to uphold the scriptures means to practice according to their teaching. Bodhisattva Jueming Miaoxing says:
“To uphold this scripture is to practice according to this scripture.”

(The Direct Pointing to the West) To uphold the precepts means to remember and hold them without forgetting, and to do no evil. “Uphold the scriptures and precepts as a poor man who has found a treasure”: this is the heart of this chapter, the World-Honored One’s revelation of the utmost compassion. When a poor man obtains a treasure, all his sufferings at once cease, and from then on he is joyful and free of care. This uses a treasure as a simile for the wondrous function of the scriptures and precepts. Moreover, since the poor man has obtained the treasure, it is bound up with his very life, and he should guard it with all his strength and never lose it. This exhorts practitioners who have received the scriptures and precepts to uphold them well, as they would guard their own lives. If they transgress, they should repent at once and vow never to do so again. “Wash (
xǐ
) the mind and change your conduct”: to wash away the evil thoughts in the mind and reform utterly. “Zhé”: always.

“Wherever the Buddha walks, in countries and cities, in villages and hamlets, none fail to receive his transformation. The world is harmonious and compliant, the sun and moon are clear and bright. Wind and rain come in season, and calamity and pestilence do not arise. The country is rich and the people at peace, and weapons are of no use. Virtue is honored and benevolence promoted, and all apply themselves to courtesy and yielding. In the land there are no thieves, and no injustice or wrong. The strong do not oppress the weak, and each finds his place.”

Wherever the Buddha walks, in countries (states) and cities (towns), in villages (districts) and hamlets (villages), none fail to receive the Buddha’s transformation. The world is harmonious and compliant, the sun and moon are clear and bright. Wind and rain come in season, and calamity and pestilence (disaster and plague) do not arise. The country is rich and the people at peace, and there is no war. Virtue is honored and benevolence promoted, and all apply themselves to practicing courtesy and yielding. In the land there are no thieves, and no injustice or wrong. The strong do not oppress the weak, and each finds his place.
“Mǐ”: not any; none.

“I pity you all more than parents think on their children. I become a Buddha in this world, and with good do battle against evil, uprooting the suffering of birth-and-death. I cause you to obtain the five virtues and rise to the peace of non-doing. When I enter parinirvāṇa, the scriptures and the Way will gradually be extinguished. The people will be flattering and false, and will do every evil again. The five burnings and five pains will, as time goes on, grow ever fiercer. You should teach and admonish one another, and according to the Buddha’s scriptures and Dharma, you must not transgress.”

I pity you all more than parents think on their children. I become a Buddha in this world, and with good do battle against evil, uprooting the suffering of birth-and-death. I cause you to obtain the five virtues (namely the five goods spoken of above: not killing, not stealing, not committing sexual misconduct, not speaking falsely, and not drinking alcohol) and to rise to the peace of non-doing. After my parinirvāṇa, the scriptures and the Way will gradually be extinguished. The people will be flattering and false (sycophantic and deceitful), and will do every evil again. The five pains and five burnings will, as time goes on, grow ever fiercer. You should teach and admonish one another, and strictly observe the Buddha’s scriptures and Dharma, and must not transgress.

“Parinirvāṇa”: rendered in Chinese as “entering extinction,” or briefly “nirvāṇa.” “The scriptures and the Way will gradually be extinguished”: the True Dharma of Śākyamuni Buddha lasts five hundred years, the Semblance Dharma a thousand years, and the Final Dharma ten thousand years; when all these have passed, it is called the complete extinction of the scriptures and the Way.

“Bodhisattva Maitreya, with palms joined, spoke: The evil and suffering of the people of the world are just so, just so. The Buddha in his compassion pities them all and delivers them all. We have received the Buddha’s repeated teachings, and dare not transgress or lose them.”
